title: Cotton Stalk to Pellets
subtitle: Replicable case study & district implementation roadmap for Andhra Pradesh
audience: For cotton-major districts: Kurnool/Nandyal, Guntur/Palnadu/NTR, Anantapur, Prakasam and adjoining clusters
source_note: Sources: CAI/Cottonguru URJA Project case study; ICAR-CIRCOT logistics model; ANGRAU cotton outlook.

blocks.text: Field residue → clean fuel → soil carbon → income

sections.title: 1. Why this matters in Andhra Pradesh
sections.lead: Cotton stalk is not just waste — it is a district-level feedstock for energy, soil improvement and incomes.
sections.source: Sources: CAI issue No. 25, p.4; ANGRAU Cotton Outlook 2022.

items.label: AP cotton pressing estimate for 2023–24 in CAI table
Kurnool, Guntur, Anantapur, Krishna and Prakasam covered most AP cotton acreage in ANGRAU outlook
stalks can become pellets, briquettes, biochar and carbon credits

blocks.text: The usual end-of-season problem: stalks occupy fields, removal is laborious, burning causes local air pollution, and farmers receive no value.
The opportunity: organise post-harvest collection through FPOs/SHGs, chip within villages, and link to nearby pellet/briquette units or industrial users.

blocks.title: District lens
items: Cotton clusters have concentrated, seasonal feedstock.
Ginning/power/brick/thermal users create local demand.
District administration can reduce open burning while adding farm income.

sections.title: 2. Case study: URJA Project in Yavatmal
sections.lead: Cottonguru MahaFPO Federation model converts cotton stalks into pellets, biochar and carbon-credit-linked value.
sections.source: Source: Cotton Association of India, Cotton Statistics & News, 17 Sept 2024, pp.1–3.

blocks.title: Case study outcomes mentioned in the document
items: Pellet-based cooking systems reduce indoor smoke exposure by about 90%.
Pellets are reported as about 50% cheaper than LPG for participating communities.
Biochar use: 20% cotton yield improvement, 10% lower fertilizer use and 15% lower water consumption.
About 1,000 tribal women engaged in production/distribution in the Yavatmal region.

sections.title: 3. Technology pathway: stalk → pellets + biochar + credits
sections.lead: Simple field logistics plus local processing creates multiple outputs from the same biomass stream.
sections.source: Sources: ICAR-CIRCOT logistics model; CAI/Cottonguru URJA case study.

stages.name: Dry
stages.desc: sun drying near field / collection point

blocks.title: Key technology choices for districts
items: Mobile pelletizer units can reach distant farms where transport is difficult.
Biochar is produced through carbon-stabilizing processing and can be applied back to cotton soils.
Industrial buyers can use pellets/briquettes as renewable process heat fuel.

blocks.title: What district officials should standardize
items: Residue collection protocol
Moisture and chip-size specifications
Factory-gate weighing and digital payments
Fire-safety and storage norms

sections.title: 4. Logistics model: the missing link solved
sections.lead: CIRCOT identifies logistics—not pellet technology alone—as the key barrier to cotton stalk utilisation.
sections.source: Source: ICAR-CIRCOT, “Logistics Model for Cotton Stalk Supply for Preparation of Briquettes and Pellets”, pp.1–3.

blocks.title: CIRCOT model
items: Uproot stalks from field with tractor-operated V-type uprooter.
Sun dry the uprooted stalks near the field.
Shred/chip with tractor-operated shredder.
Transport chipped stalks to pellet/briquette plant within a 50 km radius.

blocks.text: Why it fits AP: existing tractors, custom-hiring centres, FPO networks and ginning clusters can be used to organise the seasonal collection window.

sections.title: 5. Business case: value is created at several points
sections.lead: A district programme should keep value local: farmers earn, rural youth operate logistics, women SHGs manage distribution and plants get feedstock.
sections.source: Sources: ICAR-CIRCOT logistics model; CAI/Cottonguru URJA case study.

blocks.footnote: Illustrative value from CIRCOT logistics model

blocks.text: Potential farmer margin: about ₹1,500–2,000 per tonne before local arrangements for service providers.

items.desc: Fuel for cooking or process heat

blocks.text: For AP, pilot contracts should specify: price to farmers, service fee for machine owners, plant off-take commitment and quality deductions.
Districts can use the first season to establish reliable tonnage data for later carbon or CSR-linked scaling.

sections.title: 6. Priority AP districts and cluster logic
sections.lead: Start where feedstock is concentrated and nearby demand/off-take can be anchored.
sections.source: Source basis: ANGRAU Cotton Outlook 2022; ICAR-CIRCOT logistics model; recent AP cotton reporting. District names reflect current AP district structure where relevant.

rows: Large cotton concentration; tractors and CHCs can support collection.
Cotton markets/ginning ecosystem and accessible industrial buyers.
Seasonal residue aggregation potential near transport corridors.
Any mandal with ≥2,000–3,000 ha cotton cluster
Use 50 km radius to link villages to one plant or mobile pelletizer.

blocks.title: Selection criteria for each district
items: Cotton acreage within contiguous mandals
Distance to pellet/briquette/industrial heat user
FPO/SHG readiness to aggregate biomass
Availability of tractors, uprooters and shredders
Safe storage yards and road access

blocks.text: Recommendation: begin with 2–3 clusters per priority district, each designed around one 50 km collection radius and one anchor buyer.

sections.title: 7. Benefits for district administration
sections.lead: The programme can align environment, agriculture, livelihoods and local industry priorities.
sections.source: Source basis: benefits adapted from CAI/Cottonguru URJA case study and ICAR-CIRCOT logistics model.

items.desc: Reduced open burning and smoke during post-harvest season
Extra value from stalks that are otherwise a disposal cost
Aggregation, quality checks, packaging, distribution and machine operation
Biochar can help improve soil fertility and reduce water/fertilizer need
Pellets/briquettes can replace part of fossil fuel or firewood demand
Biochar carbon removal pathway can attract CSR/carbon-credit partners

blocks.text: District KPI suggestion: tonnes collected, farmer payments, acres covered, women/youth enterprises created, emissions avoided, pellets sold, biochar applied.

sections.title: 8. District implementation model
sections.lead: Create a reliable biomass supply chain before scaling pellet or biochar capacity.
sections.source: Source basis: ICAR-CIRCOT logistics model and URJA community/FPO model.

blocks.title: District administration role
items: Notify pilot mandals and create residue aggregation calendar.
Converge Agriculture, DRDA/SHG, Pollution Control, Industries and Energy departments.
Facilitate buyer MoUs and common weighing/quality protocol.

blocks.title: Operating safeguards
items: Storage yards away from houses and power lines.
Moisture specification to prevent fungal/fire risk.
Transparent grade deductions and payment timelines.
No diversion of essential fodder where relevant.

blocks.text: Use one nodal officer and one district dashboard. Without tonnage, payment and buyer data, scaling will fail.

sections.title: 9. Governance and partnerships
sections.lead: A district mission structure can convert a pilot into a bankable, replicable programme.
sections.source: Source basis: institutional suggestions adapted for Andhra Pradesh from CIRCOT and URJA case study models.

items.desc: approve pilot, convene departments, monitor KPIs
training, crop cluster mapping, farmer mobilization
off-take, quality specs, storage and processing
fuel buyers: boilers, hostels, kitchens, brick kilns
biochar MRV, carbon credit readiness, buyer financing

blocks.text: Recommended structure: District Cotton Stalk Utilisation Cell with a weekly 30-minute review during the harvest/residue collection window.

sections.title: 10. 90-day pilot plan for one district
sections.lead: Aim: prove tonnage, payments, quality and buyer acceptance in one collection season.
sections.source: Source basis: implementation plan adapted from CIRCOT logistics steps and URJA social-enterprise model.

groups.label: Days 0–15
groups.name: Preparation
tasks: Select mandals, map cotton acreage, identify FPO/SHG aggregators and buyer/off-taker.

groups.label: Days 16–30
groups.name: Readiness
tasks: Finalize prices, service charges, storage yards, machines and safety protocol.

groups.label: Days 31–60
groups.name: Field operations
tasks: Uproot, dry, chip and transport stalks; digital weighment and farmer payment.

groups.label: Days 61–75
groups.name: Processing
tasks: Pellet/briquette trial production; test moisture, bulk density and combustion use.

groups.label: Days 76–90
groups.name: Scale decision
tasks: Publish pilot report; approve next-season scale-up and financing needs.

blocks.text: Pilot target suggestion: 2–3 mandal clusters, 1 anchor buyer, 1 machine-service group per cluster and daily tonnage/payment tracking.

sections.title: 11. Ask from district officials
sections.lead: A small, well-governed pilot can unlock a statewide cotton-stalk bioenergy programme.
sections.source: Prepared from provided case studies: CAI/Cottonguru URJA Project and ICAR-CIRCOT Logistics Model.

items.title: Approve district pilot
items.body: Identify 2–3 mandal clusters and one nodal officer for the 90-day pilot.

items.title: Convene partners
items.body: Bring FPOs, SHGs, CHCs, pellet units, ginners, industrial users and KVK/technical experts to one table.

items.title: Enable market signal
items.body: Issue transparent price, quality, storage and payment protocol; sign buyer MoUs before collection starts.

blocks.title: Next step
items: Prepare a one-page district cotton-stalk resource map.
Select pilot villages and machine owners before harvest end.
Collect data from day one: tonnes, moisture, payments, costs and buyers.
Use the pilot report to propose district/state budget, CSR and carbon finance support.
